system: You are a technical assistant. Reply concisely.
prompt: Explain in detail how a memory-bounded Mixture-of-Experts inference engine achieves sub-linear physical memory growth while keeping dense attention layers fully resident. Start from the MoE layer structure: a router (gate) produces per-token logits over N experts, and the top-k experts are selected for each token. In a naive implementation every expert weight tensor is loaded into RAM together with the dense backbone, so the resident set equals the whole model. The key observation is that at any given decoding step only a small subset of experts is actually used, and the same few experts tend to be reused across consecutive tokens because of locality in the router distribution. This suggests an on-demand residency model: keep the dense tensors and the router always resident, but treat expert weights as evictable pages managed by a bounded-capacity pool. A practical pool is a contiguous memory arena split into slots; each slot can hold one expert weight tensor (or a slice of it). A scheduler maintains a mapping from (layer, expert) to its current slot, plus a reuse counter used for eviction decisions. When a token routes to an expert that is not resident, the scheduler issues an asynchronous read of that expert bytes from the model file (bypassing the page cache using unbuffered direct I/O on Windows, with sector-aligned reads and a dedicated thread pool). While the read is in flight, the compute graph for the token is stalled only on the attention part; the expert computation waits on the slot readiness. If the pool is full, the scheduler evicts the least-recently-used expert whose slot is not currently referenced by an in-flight graph, and reuses that slot for the incoming expert. Eviction is free because expert weights are read-only: we never write them back, we simply drop the slot mapping. To hide latency, reads for the next few tokens can be prefetched by looking at the router output of the current token; because router outputs are themselves cheap, the scheduler can issue prefetch reads before the current step finishes. The pool budget is a single configurable number, so the operator can cap peak resident memory regardless of model size. For a model with 128 experts per layer and 43 layers, resident expert memory is bounded by the pool size rather than by the product of expert count and per-expert weight bytes. The dense part (attention, norms, embeddings, LM head) stays mmap-backed read-only and resident only on first touch. When the GPU is available, the dense layers can be offloaded while the expert pool stays on CPU, giving a hybrid placement that reduces host memory traffic for attention. The scheduler also exposes statistics per expert: request count, resident time, miss count, and average load latency, which feed an offline simulator to tune the pool size. One subtlety is that the MoE expert tensors in the GGUF file are laid out in a different order than the compute graph expects (gate_up and down interleaved by expert), so a converter rearranges the tensor layout so each expert is contiguous and page-aligned, enabling single-read loads. Another subtlety is that quantized experts (Q8_0 or Q4_K) have non-trivial block layouts; the pool slot must account for the quantization block size and alignment so the compute kernel can read the resident bytes directly without a repack step. The async loader uses Win32 OVERLAPPED I/O on a completion port; each read is a single IOCTL with no intermediate staging buffer, so bytes land directly in the slot (zero-copy). If the kernel needs a different data layout than the file layout, the loader performs an in-place transcode in the slot while the previous kernel still runs, double-buffered to avoid stalling. The system was validated by comparing prefill hidden states and sampled tokens against a stock build with the same inputs; cosine similarity of every layer output stays above 0.99 and the generated text is token-identical for temperature zero. Explain the trade-off between slot size (whole expert vs per-layer slice) and fragmentation: larger slots reduce the number of IO requests but waste memory when experts vary in size, while smaller slots increase scheduler overhead. Describe how the eviction policy interacts with the router locality: if the router is biased toward a few hot experts, the pool effectively becomes a cache with very high hit rate and the miss penalty is amortized by prefetching. Finally, walk through a concrete decoding step for a 128-expert, 43-layer model: which tensors are resident, which are read on demand, how the graph is split into dense (attention) and expert (pool) sections, and how the two sections are synchronized with an event so the pipeline never blocks on the slower of the two.
